title: Reduction to a principal complete normal counterexample to quasi-excellence lifting
statement: Let $A$ be a commutative Noetherian $\mathbf Q$-algebra [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], complete for an ideal $I$ [def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring]. Suppose $A/I$ is quasi-excellent but $A$ is not [def-exc-excellent-ring]. Then there exist a commutative Noetherian normal Nagata $\mathbf Q$-domain $R$ and a nonzero nonunit $x\in R$ such that $R$ is $(x)$-adically complete, universally catenary, not quasi-excellent, and $R/K$ is quasi-excellent for every nonzero ideal $K\subseteq R$. Normal and Nagata have the meanings of [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring, def-weil-pbc-nagata-ring]. For every finite field extension $L/\operatorname{Frac}R$, its integral closure $B_L$ of $R$ [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure] is finite as an $R$-module, normal, Nagata, universally catenary and $(x)$-adically complete; $B_L/xB_L$ is quasi-excellent, and for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak n\subset B_L$ the maximal-ideal completion $\widehat{(B_L)_{\mathfrak n}}$ is a normal local domain [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime, def-weil-pbc-adic-completion].

source.place: Kurano–Shimomoto, Ideal-adic completion of quasi-excellent rings (after Gabber), Theorem 5.1, Step 1 (1-1)–(1-4), printed pp.7–8; finite normalization properties recalled in Step 2, (5.3), and Step 3; obtained in sandbox sources/kurano40.pdf (bibliographic integration requested in report.md).

proof.text: Write $I=(a_1,\ldots,a_t)$ and $I_i=(a_1,\ldots,a_i)$. Each $A/I_i$ is complete for the image of $I$, since it is a finite $A$-module, and hence for the subideal generated by the image of $a_{i+1}$. The sequence begins with a non-quasi-excellent ring and ends with a quasi-excellent ring, so choose adjacent terms with the latter property first appearing. Put $C=A/I_i$ and $x=a_{i+1}\bmod I_i$. Then $C$ is $(x)$-complete, not quasi-excellent, and $C/xC$ is quasi-excellent. Here $x\ne0$, since otherwise the adjacent terms coincide; $x$ is a nonunit since $(x)$ lies in the Jacobson radical of the nonzero complete ring $C$. Quotients remain Noetherian: lift ideal generators from $A$.

Among the ideals $J\subset C$ with $C/J$ not quasi-excellent choose a maximal one, using the maximal condition for submodules of the finite $C$-module $C$. Put $D=C/J$. It is Noetherian, $(x)$-complete, and not quasi-excellent. Every nonzero ideal $H\subset D$ pulls back to an ideal strictly containing $J$, so $D/H$ is quasi-excellent. Moreover $D/xD=C/(J+xC)$ is a quotient of $C/xC$, hence quasi-excellent by finite-type stability on spectra, applied to $\operatorname{Spec}(C/(J+xC))\to\operatorname{Spec}(C/xC)$. Its hypothesis that every affine open of $Y=\operatorname{Spec}(C/xC)$ has quasi-excellent ring holds: $Y$ is locally Noetherian by its one-chart cover [pqf-def-locnoeth], and the cover-locality lemmas [lem-trf-g-ring-affine-cover, lem-trf-j2-affine-cover] applied to that cover give the G-ring and J-2 properties on every affine open, which is Noetherian as a G-ring. The same check applies to every affine base below. Thus $x\ne0$ in $D$, and completeness again makes it a nonunit.

The complete ideal $(x)$ lies in every maximal ideal of $D$. If $D$ were a G-ring, the Jacobson-quotient criterion would make $D$ quasi-excellent, a contradiction. The pair-of-primes criterion therefore supplies primes $Q\subseteq P$ whose quotient generic formal fibre is not geometrically regular. If $Q\ne0$, then $D/Q$ is quasi-excellent by the preceding maximality, so is a G-ring and that same criterion makes this fibre geometrically regular, a contradiction. Hence $Q=0$ is prime, so $D$ is a domain.

Since $D/xD$ is quasi-excellent it is Nagata, and Nagata lifting makes $D$ Nagata. Let $R$ be its integral closure in $\operatorname{Frac}D$. The N-2 property, applied to the identity extension of fraction fields, makes $R$ finite over $D$, and the integral-closure lemma makes it a normal domain. It is Noetherian and Nagata by finite-algebra permanence, and $(x)$-complete by finite-module completeness. Lying over makes $\operatorname{Spec}R\to\operatorname{Spec}D$ surjective. If $R$ were quasi-excellent, finite-surjective descent would make $D$ quasi-excellent. Thus $R$ is not quasi-excellent. It is still a $\mathbf Q$-algebra and $x\ne0$; completeness makes $x$ a nonunit.

For a nonzero ideal $K\subset R$ choose $0

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 1 (1-3), preservation of (A2) under normalization, printed p.8

proof.text: Fix any finite extension $L/\operatorname{Frac}R$ and let $B_L$ be the integral closure. Since $R$ is Nagata its N-2 property makes $B_L$ finite over $R$. The integral-closure lemma makes $B_L$ a normal domain with fraction field $L$. Finite-algebra permanence makes it Noetherian and Nagata, and finite-module completeness makes it $(x)$-complete. The quotient $B_L/xB_L$ is a finite algebra over $R/xR$ and is therefore quasi-excellent. Apply normal-completion lifting to $B_L$ with ideal $xB_L$: for every prime $\mathfrak p$ of $B_L$, the completion of $(B_L)_{\mathfrak p}$ is a normal local domain. This supplies, in particular, all the requested maximal-ideal completions.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 1 (1-4) and Step 2 through (5.3), printed pp.8–9

proof.text: Apply the preceding argument also with $L=\operatorname{Frac}R$, for which $B_L=R$ by normality. For $T=R$ or any $B_L$ and any prime $\mathfrak p\subset T$, the localization $T_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Noetherian domain, and its completion is a domain, hence has a single irreducible component; its Krull dimension equals $\dim T_{\mathfrak p}$ and is finite by [lem-weil-pbc-completion-dimension], so the spectrum is equidimensional. The sole minimal prime of $T_{\mathfrak p}$ is zero. The Ratliff criterion therefore makes every $T_{\mathfrak p}$ universally catenary.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 1 (1-4), printed p.8 (Ratliff criterion; Stacks Tag 0AW6)

proof.text: This implies universal catenarity of $T$. Indeed, in a finite-type $T$-algebra $E$, take primes $\mathfrak a\subseteq\mathfrak b$ and put $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak b\cap T$. Every prime in the interval $[\mathfrak a,\mathfrak b]$ avoids $T\setminus\mathfrak p$. Localizing at this set therefore gives an order isomorphism of the entire prime interval with its image in the finite-type $T_{\mathfrak p}$-algebra $E\otimes_TT_{\mathfrak p}$. The inverse sends a localized prime to its contraction: for a prime avoiding this set, $a/s$ is in its extension exactly when $a$ is in the prime, since the denominator and every multiplier from the set avoid the prime. These inverse inclusion-preserving maps preserve lengths and saturation of chains. Catenarity of that algebra supplies both the finite bound and equality of saturated lengths in the original interval. Thus $T$ is universally catenary, by its definition, for both $R$ and every $B_L$. All required properties now hold.

source.place: Theorem 5.1, Step 1 (1-4), local-to-global universal catenarity (Stacks algebra.tex Tag 0AUN)
